item.title: Fiji must represent itself with dignity at overseas meets – Minister Ditoka
item.description: Foreign Affairs and External Trade Minister Sakiasi Ditoka says Fiji must strike a balance between responsible spending and ensuring its leaders are adequately supported when representing the country overseas. Mr Ditoka made the comments in response to reports the President is representing Fiji at the United Nations General Assembly.
item.content:encoded:
Foreign Affairs and External Trade Minister Sakiasi Ditoka says Fiji must strike a balance between responsible spending and ensuring its leaders are adequately supported when representing the country overseas.

Mr Ditoka made the comments in response to reports the President is representing Fiji at the United Nations General Assembly.

He said the President, as Fiji’s Head of State and holder of the country’s highest office, should receive arrangements that reflected the dignity and standing of the office.

“When the President represents Fiji internationally, the arrangements made should properly reflect the dignity and standing of that Office and of the Republic itself,” Mr Ditoka said.

He said the same principle should apply proportionately to other government representatives travelling overseas, including the Prime Minister, ministers and ambassadors.

“This is not an argument for extravagance,” Mr Ditoka said.

“Public funds must always be used responsibly, and official travel must be reasonable, necessary and within the means available to Government.”

However, he said responsible expenditure should not result in Fiji inadequately supporting officials tasked with representing the country internationally.

“There must be a sensible balance,” he said.

Mr Ditoka acknowledged Fiji was a small developing country and that taxpayers ultimately carried the cost of official overseas travel.

“At the same time, Fiji is a sovereign nation. When our representatives engage other governments and international institutions, they carry the name and interests of our country with them,” he said.

Mr Ditoka said the level of protocol, security, logistical and official support provided should reflect the position held and the nature of the international engagement.

“Our approach should therefore be straightforward: no extravagance and no unnecessary expenditure, but neither should we diminish the dignity of our national institutions or compromise the ability of our representatives to do their work effectively,” he said.

“We should represent Fiji well, within reason and within our means.”

item.title: Supreme court restores conviction
item.description: The Supreme Court has restored the conviction and sentence of Joshua Rahman after allowing the State’s petition against a Court of Appeal decision that had quashed his conviction and ordered a retrial. Supreme Court Justice Anthony Gates delivered the judgment in Suva today.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court has restored the conviction and sentence of Joshua Rahman after allowing the State’s petition against a Court of Appeal decision that had quashed his conviction and ordered a retrial.

Supreme Court Justice Anthony Gates delivered the judgment in Suva today.

Rahman had been convicted under Section 5A of the Illicit Drugs Control Act 2004 and Section 46 of the Crimes Act 2009.

In its earlier ruling, the High Court had imposed a 23-year prison sentence, which, after taking into account the time he had already spent in custody, resulted in a total non-parole period of 14 years.

The Court of Appeal later quashed the conviction and sentence and ordered that Rahman be retried as soon as possible.

On April 10, 2026, Rahman’s lawyers lodged a petition in the Supreme Court seeking to have the retrial order set aside and, instead, an order of acquittal.

The State had lodged its own petition on March 13, 2026.

A central issue before the Supreme Court concerned Section 32 of the Illicit Drugs Control Act, which provides for a factual presumption of possession.

The court heard that once it was proved that drugs found on premises were under the control of an accused, the law raised a presumption that the accused was in possession of those drugs until the presumption was rebutted.

Under the approach applied at the time of the High Court judgment, the burden placed on the accused was on the balance of probabilities.

However, the Court of Appeal, after considering decisions from other jurisdictions, subsequently determined that Section 32 had to be read down to impose a lesser burden, so that it was consistent with the Constitution.

In effect, the accused only had to discharge an evidential burden by calling or pointing to evidence capable of raising a reasonable doubt as to whether he was in possession of the illicit drugs.

The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge had applied the incorrect burden to the defence and, as a result, quashed Rahman’s conviction and sentence and ordered an expedited retrial.

The Supreme Court, however, found that the High Court judge had been correct on the evidence in finding against Rahman and that the prosecution had proved its case against him beyond reasonable doubt.

The case concerned 39 kilograms of cocaine found during a police raid at premises where Rahman and his father, Talat Rahman, were living.

Evidence was led that Talat had pleaded guilty in New Zealand in two cases involving the importation of drugs into that country. The issue before the court was whether Rahman had lent support or assistance to his father in the possession of the cocaine and whether joint control of the Caubati Road premises had been established.

The Supreme Court found that, on the evidence, the High Court judge was correct in finding against Rahman and that the case had been proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The court noted that the judge had approached the case with the prosecution’s burden in mind.

anThe Supreme Court consequently made five orders. It granted special leave for both petitions, dismissed Rahman’s petition, allowed the State’s petition, quashed the decision of the Court of Appeal, and restored Rahman’s conviction and sentence in the High Court.

item.title: Milestone for clan
item.description: THE Tokatoka Sautorotoro of Korovuto Village is expanding its business operations, marking a new chapter in its efforts to create long-term economic opportunities for its members. The landowning unit officially opened a new Nadi office for its business arm, Infinity Pacific Pte Ltd.
item.content:encoded:
THE Tokatoka Sautorotoro of Korovuto Village is expanding its business operations, marking a new chapter in its efforts to create long-term economic opportunities for its members.

The landowning unit officially opened a new Nadi office for its business arm, Infinity Pacific Pte Ltd.

Officiating at the event was iTaukei Land Trust Board CEO Solomone Nata, who said the milestone demonstrated the commitment of Tokatoka Sautorotoro to move beyond relying solely on lease income and instead invest in sustainable business ventures.

“Tokatoka Sautorotoro stands as an example of what can be achieved when we shift our mindset from simply receiving lease funds to actively creating wealth and opportunities for our people,” he said.

Mr Nata congratulated the trustees and tokatoka members for their vision, determination and commitment to building a business that would provide direct benefits to their community.

He said the new office represented more than an expansion of the company’s physical presence.

“The opening of this office represents more than just a new building. It is a symbol of what can be achieved through strong leadership, collaboration and a shared commitment to creating a better future for our communities.”

The landowners acknowledged the support of the TLTB, particularly through its Taukei Development Fund Facility.

Through the facility, Infinity Pacific was able to access financing, with repayments secured through an assignment of 30 per cent of lease proceeds.

Mr Nata said the funding had helped the company strengthen and expand its operations since its incorporation in 2023.

The company began with two Ace vans, providing transportation transfers and tours before expanding into property development and other services to meet the growing demands of Fiji’s tourism industry.

Mr Nata said the company’s growth reflected the entrepreneurial spirit of the members of Tokatoka Sautorotoro.

“This achievement is a true testament to vision, discipline and the entrepreneurial spirit of the iTaukei people, particularly the members of Tokatoka Sautorotoro.”

He said the continued expansion of Infinity Pacific’s transport fleet would increase the company’s capacity, create more employment opportunities and strengthen its contribution to the tourism sector in Nadi.

The opening of the new office marks another step in Tokatoka Sautorotoro’s efforts to turn its land resources into sustainable economic opportunities for future generations.

item.title: Sentence slashed over error
item.description: A MAN convicted of aggravated robbery has had his prison sentence reduced by six months after the High Court found that the magistrate failed to account for the time he had already spent in custody before trial. Justice Lee James Burney allowed Saimone Banuve’s appeal against sentence after the court was told he spent six months in remand from August 26, 2019 to February 26, 2020.
item.content:encoded:
A MAN convicted of aggravated robbery has had his prison sentence reduced by six months after the High Court found that the magistrate failed to account for the time he had already spent in custody before trial.

Justice Lee James Burney allowed Saimone Banuve’s appeal against sentence after the court was told he spent six months in remand from August 26, 2019 to February 26, 2020.

Banuve was convicted of aggravated robbery following a trial and sentenced last year to 24 months’ imprisonment with a non-parole period of 12 months.

The judge found it was an error of law for the magistrate not to expressly consider the six months Banuve had spent in remand, as required under section 24 of the Sentencing and Penalties Act 2009.

The court noted the magistrate may have not been made aware of the appellant’s earlier period in custody.

The court quashed the original sentence and substituted it with 18 months’ imprisonment, with a non-parole period of six months, effective from July 21, 2025.

item.title: Man to serve 12 months in prison
item.description: A MAN, who stabbed his wife multiple times during an argument at their Vatuwaqa, Suva home, has been sentenced to three years imprisonment. Justice Thushara Rajasinghe sentenced the man last month after he pleaded guilty to one count of act intended to cause grievous harm.
item.content:encoded:
A MAN, who stabbed his wife multiple times during an argument at their Vatuwaqa, Suva home, has been sentenced to three years imprisonment.

Justice Thushara Rajasinghe sentenced the man last month after he pleaded guilty to one count of act intended to cause grievous harm.

The court was told the couple were arguing over the accused’s interaction with another person during a drinking party at their home on November 10, 2024. The argument continued after the man went to the kitchen to prepare food and escalated when he took a kitchen knife and stabbed his wife multiple times under her breasts.

She suffered severe injuries and was rushed to the hospital.

Justice Rajasinghe partly suspended the sentence, whereby the man will serve 18 months, and the remaining months are suspended for a period of three years.

After considering the nearly 195 days he had already spent in custody, the man will serve an actual 12 months in prison.

item.title: Exercise Bougainville ’26
item.description: THE Republic of Fiji Military Forces conducted the last stage of Exercise Bougainville 2026 near Vuda Marina and Serenity Island on Tuesday. The major brigade-level training operation, running from August 10 to 28, has featured the frequent movement of naval vessels, water police, and armed personnel. Communities near the exercise zones were issued advance notices to prepare for simulated battle n
item.content:encoded:
THE Republic of Fiji Military Forces conducted the last stage of Exercise Bougainville 2026 near Vuda Marina and Serenity Island on Tuesday.

The major brigade-level training operation, running from August 10 to 28, has featured the frequent movement of naval vessels, water police, and armed personnel. Communities near the exercise zones were issued advance notices to prepare for simulated battle noise, including blank ammunition, pyrotechnics, and heavy explosive sound effects.

Military officials said the multi-agency deployment was crucial for evaluating national defence coordination and operational readiness throughout the scheduled two-week window.

The exercises ensure our forces maintain the highest standards of preparedness and interagency collaboration.

The comprehensive training brings together key national institutions, including the Civil Aviation Authority of Fiji, the Ministry of Health, the Fiji Navy, and the Fiji Police Force. Representatives and observers from the Australian Defence Force and the New Zealand Defence Force are also participating to foster regional security partnerships.

RFMF troops marched from the Waikamu industrial area located at the Nadi Town end, through Nadi Town and concluded at King Charles Park to mark the end of Exercise Bougainville 2026.

item.title: Methodist conference rings with hymns
item.description: THE Vodafone Arena in Suva comes alive each evening with the sound of hymns, as 130 choirs from across Fiji gather to raise their voices in songs at the Methodist Church’s week-long annual conference. From cherished traditional hymns to contemporary arrangements, the music resonates with themes of faith, unity and devotion.
item.content:encoded:
THE Vodafone Arena in Suva comes alive each evening with the sound of hymns, as 130 choirs from across Fiji gather to raise their voices in songs at the Methodist Church’s week-long annual conference.

From cherished traditional hymns to contemporary arrangements, the music resonates with themes of faith, unity and devotion.

The celebration extends beyond church choirs, with schools, civil servants also taking part through the institutions and ministries they serve.

Together, the voices of the faithful create a moving celebration of fellowship, worship and the unifying power of music.

item.title: Tourism earnings
item.description: THE tourism sector is expected to reach $4 billion in tourism earnings by 2027, alongside an increase in visitor arrivals to 1.25 million. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka shared this during an event on Wednesday night where Warwick Hotels and Resorts announced it was to opening its capital base to Fijian investors.
item.content:encoded:
THE tourism sector is expected to reach $4 billion in tourism earnings by 2027, alongside an increase in visitor arrivals to 1.25 million.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka shared this during an event on Wednesday night where Warwick Hotels and Resorts announced it was to opening its capital base to Fijian investors.

Mr Rabuka said achieving the earnings target would require continued investment in tourism, including developments by investors such as Warwick Hotels and Resorts, and an increase of about 4000 hotel rooms across Fiji.

“The timing of these developments couldn’t be better,” he said.

Mr Rabuka said new tourism developments would create opportunities beyond hotel construction, including employment, careers for young people and business opportunities for farmers, fishermen, transport operators, tradespeople and small businesses.

He said Fiji welcomed a record 986,367 visitors last year, but the achievement also placed greater responsibility on the country to continue investing in accommodation, infrastructure, aviation, service standards and its people.

“We must keep improving while protecting what makes our country special and our growth must be sustainable and must benefit our communities.”

Mr Rabuka said Fiji also needed to remain competitive as other destinations continued to invest in their tourism sectors.

He said Warwick’s decision to continue investing in Fiji reflected confidence in the country, its stability, workers and spirit.

“For our future, governments task is keep earning confidence in the tourism sector, through sound policies, good infrastructure, and a business environment that is efficient and responsive.”
